To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the immune responses of school children in southeast England to mycobacteria other that M. tuberculosis were more prevalent than to M. tuberculosis, particularly to species in the MAIS complex.
the immune responses of children to M. tuberculosis and other environmental mycobacterial species were investigated.

(1) the immune responses of school children in southeast England to M. tuberculosis and other mycobacterial species were studied prior to BCG vaccination; (2) IFN‐γ responses and skin test responses were detected to M. tuberculosis; (3) IFN responses were detected to PPDs of mycobacteria from the MAIS complex, M. marinum and other environmental mycobacterial species, but not to those from the MAC complex or M. kansas
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immune responses to mycobacteria in a group of schoolchildren in the United Kingdom, prior to BCG vaccination.
the immune responses of school children in southeast England to mycobacterial antigens.
the development of new diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IFN‐γ test is not suitable for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infection in children.
the IFN‐γ assay has been shown to be a sensitive, specific and reproducible test for measuring T‐cell responses to M. bovis and M. tuberculosis.
the Heaf skin test is the only reliable test for BCG vaccination, but that it is not a reliable test for the presence of infection with M. tuberculosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of the children in our study had been infected with mycobacteria other that M. tuberculosis, and that these infections were more common than M. tuberculosis infection, as determined by IFN‐γ assays.

the IFN‐γ assay is a useful and sensitive tool for the detection of previous infection with M. tuberculosis in a population, and can be used to identify those children who are not tuberculin‐reactive.
in a population of schoolchildren in a country with a low incidence of tuberculosis, a significant proportion of individuals have been exposed to environmental mycobacteria other M. tuberculosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the majority of schoolchildren in England have not been exposed to M. tuberculosis, and that the majority of positive skin test responses and IFN‐gamma responses to PPD are due to environmental mycobacteria other that M. tuberculosis.
the immune responses to Mycobacteriun tuberculosis and other species are not necessarily associated.
the immune responses of children in England to environmental mycobacteria are similar to the immune responses of adults in the United Kingdom and other countries.
